newsitem.title: INDIA: India domestic coffee rates soar on low output.
newsitem.headline: India domestic coffee rates soar on low output.

text.p: Rising global prices and prospects of lower output have pushed up India's domestic coffee prices to new levels, dealers said on Monday.

"World coffee prices have risen to three-year-high levels," said dealer Mohammed Kasim, adding that this would influence prices at the weekly domestic coffee auctions and determine the prices in the retail market.

Dealers said coffee was currently quoted at the London market at $2.25 per pound, sharply up from $1 per pound in the previous year. The market had moved up by 30 cents in the past four days, they said.

The All India Coffee Merchants Association (AICMA) had in the past three months increased the price of coffee powder three times -- from 150 rupees per kg to 160 rupees on February 24, to 170 rupees on March 10 and to 180 rupees on April 21.
AICMA president R.P. Sarathy said further increases in the price would depend on global prices and the behaviour at the weekly domestic coffee auctions.
"The price depends on availability, there is some shortage due to crop fall," said B. Haldurai, consumer activist and convener of the Consumer Research and Education Centre.

India's state-run Coffee Board has scaled down its 1996/97 (Oct-Sept) production estimate to 205,000 tonnes from the previous 215,000 tonnes. But industry sources and traders expect output not to exceed 180,000 tonnes.
The Board's preliminary estimate of the 1997/98 crop was 233,000 tonnes.
"The growers siphoned off much coffee in the export market in view of high global prices," said Karim. "This created a shortage in the home market leading to a price spiral."
But Coffee Board chairman Philipose Matthai said high domestic prices had encouraged the industry to cancel export orders.

"Indian prices were higher than the world market by 50 percent for some months last year. Because of such diversion exports have fallen by 6.5 percent in volume and 15 percent in value during 1996/97 over the previous year," Matthai said.
The Coffee Board has estimated exports for 1996/97 (April-March) at 160,000 tonnes, compared with 171,000 tonnes in 1995/96.
The Board has suggested the Indian Commerce Ministry consider setting up a domestic coffee futures market. "This is essential to get increased volume of good coffee for export," Matthai said.
The Board has convened a meeting of growers, curers, roasters, exporters and traders on May 12 to consider the issue, officials said.
